newsitem.title: IRAN: Women hidden power in Iran presidential election.
newsitem.headline: Women hidden power in Iran presidential election.

text.p: The all-male contenders in Friday's Iranian presidential election have caught on to the fact that the female vote could just swing the polls their way.

In the Islamic republic's most competitive election since its 1979 revolution, four presidential candidates -- three of them Shi'ite clerics -- are eager to portray themselves as champions of womens' rights.
With analysts suggesting a tight race between former culture minister Mohammad Khatami and Parliamentary Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, womens' votes could be critical.

The appeal to the women runs from revolutionary nationalism to real issues affecting everyday life for Iran's 30 million women, including political and legal representation and social issues such as the strict dress codes under Islamic law.

"Women have always been oppressed in the West and in our country in the past ... Your participation in the presidential elections will hurt the Islamic Republic's enemies," is the message from Nateq-Nouri whose campaign literature lists his achievements in promoting women being elected to parliament and a role for women as advisers in family courts.

But behind the rhetoric Iranian women are slowly gaining a voice in the Islamic republic, centring on issues such as political power, better treatment under civil law, advancement in the workplace and more cultural freedom.
Khatami, who has promised to appoint women in his cabinet based on merit, appears to have wide support among women some of whom fear that Nateq-Nouri would tighten social freedoms.
"All the candidates know how the political support of women is more important than ever before," said Shahla Lahiji, a Tehran-based publisher.
"One of the first changes we are looking for is in the civil law. It must change and it will," Lahiji said, referring to unequal legal rights between men and women in the courts.
Women continue to have a limited role in the political decision-making process in Iran though the election of 13 women in Iran's last parliamentary election was a sign of progress.
Faezeh Hashemi, daughter of outgoing president Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and a prominent member of parliament, told a press conference it was too early for Iran to have a female president.
But she added: "I do hope and believe that we can have a woman minister and it would depend on the elected president, whoever that would be." Hashemi has campaigned for Khatami.

But the sheer uphill task of gaining real power was, to many women, starkly shown when a body of senior clerics and lawyers called the Guardian Council rejected all women candidates who had signed up to run in Friday's election.
Few women have senior positions in government departments and many complain of what in the West is described as a "glass ceiling" setting a limit on promotions in the workplace.
"I work longer hours than my male colleagues and my managers do not want to use my skills," said Maryam, a 27-year-old technician who says her employer is ignoring her skills.

Cultural freedoms, such as the ability to travel alone, and a relaxation of Islamist dress codes which force women to keep themselves covered in public under the hejab or chador, are also pressing concerns.
Although womens' issues are now on the political agenda and, unlike in Iran's neighbouring Gulf Arab states, they can actually vote, it will take some time for real change.

"Any president would be strait-jacketed within the framework of the system. So he can't do anything special for women. Minor liberties is the most he can do if he is broad minded," said one Iranian female journalist.
